title: Black Holes
tagline: From thought experiment to first image.
source: Generated from “Timeline of black hole physics” on Wikipedia; each event links to its source article.

events.title: Ismaël Bullialdus
events.text: 1640 — Ismaël Bullialdus suggests an inverse-square gravitational force law

events.title: Isaac Newton
events.text: 1684 — Isaac Newton writes down his inverse-square law of universal gravitation

events.title: John Michell predicts dark stars
events.text: John Michell predicts dark stars. John Michell proposed objects so massive that light could not escape.

references.label: Encyclopedia article: Timeline of black hole physics

events.title: Pierre Laplace
events.text: 1795 — Pierre Laplace discusses classical bodies which have escape velocities greater than the speed of light

events.title: William Kingdon Clifford
events.text: 1870 — William Kingdon Clifford suggests that the motion of matter may be due to changes in the geometry of space

events.title: Hans Reissner
events.text: 1910 — Hans Reissner and Gunnar Nordström define Reissner–Nordström singularity, Hermann Weyl solves special case for a point-body source

events.title: Karl Schwarzschild
events.text: 1916 — Karl Schwarzschild and independently Johannes Droste solve the Einstein vacuum field equations for uncharged spherically symmetric non-rotating systems

events.title: Hans Reissner
events.text: 1918 — Hans Reissner and Gunnar Nordström solve the Einstein–Maxwell field equations for charged spherically symmetric non-rotating systems

events.title: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
events.text: 1931 — Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar calculates, using special relativity, that a non-rotating body of electron-degenerate matter above a certain limiting mass (at 1.4 solar masses) has no stable solutions

events.title: Richard Chace Tolman
events.text: 1939 — Using the work of Richard Chace Tolman, Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff calculate the upper mass limit of a cold, non-rotating neutron star to be approximately 0.7 solar masses.

events.title: Maarten Schmidt
events.text: 1963 — Maarten Schmidt discovers and analyzes the first quasar, 3C 273, as a highly red-shifted active galactic nucleus, a billion light years away

events.title: Hong-Yee Chiu
events.text: 1964 — Hong-Yee Chiu coins the word quasar for a 'quasi-stellar radio source' in his article in Physics Today

events.title: Yakov Zel'dovich
events.text: 1964 — Yakov Zel'dovich and independently Edwin Salpeter propose that accretion discs around supermassive black holes are responsible for the huge amounts of energy radiated by quasars

events.title: Roger Penrose
events.text: 1965 — Roger Penrose proves that an imploding star will necessarily produce a singularity once it has formed an event horizon

events.title: Jocelyn Bell
events.text: 1967 — Jocelyn Bell discovers and analyzes the first radio pulsar, direct evidence for a neutron star

events.title: Werner Israel
events.text: 1967 — Werner Israel presents the proof of the no-hair theorem at King's College London

events.title: Roger Penrose
events.text: 1969 — Roger Penrose discusses the Penrose process for the extraction of the spin energy from a Kerr black hole

events.title: Cygnus X-1
events.text: 1972 — Identification of Cygnus X-1/HDE 226868 from dynamic observations as the first binary with a stellar black hole candidate

events.title: James Bardeen
events.text: 1972 — James Bardeen, Brandon Carter, and Stephen Hawking propose four laws of black hole mechanics in analogy with the laws of thermodynamics

events.title: James Bardeen
events.text: 1975 — James Bardeen and Jacobus Petterson show that the swirl of spacetime around a spinning black hole can act as a gyroscope stabilizing the orientation of the accretion disc and jets

events.title: microquasar
events.text: 1989 — Identification of microquasar V404 Cygni as a binary black hole candidate system

events.title: Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics
events.text: 2002 — Astronomers at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics present evidence for the hypothesis that Sagittarius A* is a supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way galaxy.

references.label: Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics

events.title: The Ohio State University
events.text: 2002 — Physicists at The Ohio State University publish fuzzball theory, which is a quantum description of black holes positing that they are extended objects composed of strings and don't have singularities.

events.title: VLBI
events.text: 2004 — One of the first VLBI observations of the black hole Sagittarius A* are made by a team that later becomes part of the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration

events.title: LIGO Scientific Collaboration
events.text: 2015 — LIGO Scientific Collaboration detects the distinctive gravitational waveforms from a binary black hole merging into a final black hole, yielding the basic parameters (e.g., distance, mass, and spin) of the three spinning black holes involved.

events.title: Sagittarius A*
events.text: 2022— Event Horizon Telescope releases the first image of the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A* at the centre of the milky way galaxy.
